chapter.title: Errors
chapter.para: Errors cross the bridge in both directions, and keep what they are: a .NET exception is a Rexx SYNTAX condition that carries the exception, and a Rexx condition is a .NET exception that carries the condition. When an error goes back to the side it came from, it is raised there as it was.

section.title: Conditions in Rexx

table.title: Errors raised in Rexx code by the bridge

row.entry: A .NET exception, thrown by the .NET code that Rexx called: the message is .NET error: type: message, and condition("O")~additional[2] is the exception itself, a NetObject, and [3] its .NET stack trace, as text (the layout of the ooRexx bridges: [1] the message, [2] the host's exception, [3] the host's traceback). A TargetInvocationException or an AggregateException with one exception is unwrapped: the exception is the one the code threw. Also the bridge's own errors (no such type, no overload accepts the arguments, an ambiguous name), without an exception.

A message that is no member of the .NET object, as for any Rexx object: Object ... does not understand message .... additional[1] is the object, [2] the message's name as Rexx sent it, and [3] a System.MissingMemberException that says what was looked for.
A wrong position for a NetArray, as for a Rexx Array ().

A Rexx condition raised in a handler or an override that .NET called, if .NET lets it out of the call that Rexx made (); also a RexxException thrown by .NET code that Rexx called, which came from Rexx code that .NET code ran ().

section.para: The helper methods of net.cls raise their errors with RAISE PROPAGATE, so the error points at the caller's line, not at net.cls.

example.title: .NET's errors in Rexx
example.programlisting:
signal on syntax say .net~System~Int32~Parse("abc") syntax: c = condition("O") say c~code .net~typeOf(c~additional[2]) say c~message say c~additional~items (c~additional[3]~pos("at System.") > 0) -- [3]: the stack trace signal on syntax name second x = .net~System~Text~StringBuilder~new~NoSuchThing second: c = condition("O") say c~code c~additional[2] .net~typeOf(c~additional[3]) say c~additional[3]~Message
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: 98.900 System.FormatException .NET error: System.FormatException: The input string 'abc' was not in a correct format. 3 1 97.1 NOSUCHTHING System.MissingMemberException System.Text.StringBuilder has no public instance member "NOSUCHTHING"

table.title: Exceptions thrown in .NET code by the bridge

row.entry: A Rexx condition (SYNTAX, HALT...) that ends a call from .NET into Rexx (Run, Send, a routine's Call; also a compile error), or that a handler or an override raised while .NET called it: ConditionName, Code ("41.1"), Rc, ErrorText, Message, Program, Line, Traceback, and the condition object (). If the condition was a 98.900 that carried a .NET exception, that exception is its InnerException.
A call into Rexx halted through its CancellationToken; its InnerException is the RexxException 4.1 ().
A Rexx result that does not convert to the type asked for (Run<int> of "abc").

section.title: Where Errors Go
section.para: Some errors have no Rexx caller to go to, or are raised in Rexx's own terms:

listitem.para: A Rexx condition in a handler that runs on a thread where no Rexx code waits for .NET (a timer's, the thread pool's) is reported on .error, as Rexx reports an untrapped error, and the program goes on ().

A .NET exception in a command handler (ADDRESS) is SYNTAX 98.900, as a .NET error anywhere; the context's RaiseError and RaiseFailure raise ERROR or FAILURE with the RC they are given, and an environment removed answers FAILURE with RC 30, as one that does not exist ().
A .NET exception in a function of the application raises SYNTAX 40.900, "Incorrect call to routine", with its message; wrong argument counts are 40.3 and 40.4 ().

A .NET exception in .NET code called from Rexx code that a .NET program runs is a 98.900 in that Rexx code, as in any Rexx program; if it leaves the Rexx code, the program gets a RexxException whose InnerException is that very exception.
